stories.creator: Kakuzō Okakura
stories.deck: From The Book of Tea.
stories.excerpt: The truly beautiful must always be in it.
stories.headline: The truly beautiful must always be in it.
stories.quote_context: Tea is a work of art and needs a master hand to bring out its noblest qualities. We have good and bad tea, as we have good and bad paintings--generally the latter. There is no single recipe for making the perfect tea, as there are no rules for producing a Titian or a Sesson. Each preparation of the leaves has its individuality, its special affinity with water and heat, its own method of telling a story. The truly beautiful must always be in it. How much do we not suffer through the constant failure of society to recognise this simple and fundamental law of art and life; Lichilai, a Sung poet, has sadly remarked that there were three most deplorable things in the world: the spoiling of fine youths through false education, the degradation of fine art through vulgar admiration, and the utter waste of fine tea through incompetent manipulation.

stories.creator: Christina Rossetti
stories.deck: A poem by Christina Rossetti.
stories.excerpt:
When I was dead, my spirit turned
To seek the much-frequented house:
I passed the door, and saw my friends
Feasting beneath green orange boughs;
From hand to hand they pushed the wine,
They sucked the pulp of plum and peach;
They sang, they jested, and they laughed,
For each was loved of each.

I listened to thier honest chat:
Said one: "To-morrow we shall be
Plod plod along the featureless sands,
And coasting miles and miles of sea."
Said one: "Before the turn of tide
We will achieve the eyrie-seat."
Said one: "To-morrow shall be like
To-day, but much more sweet."

"To-morrow," said they, strong with hope,
And dwelt upon the pleasant way:
"To-morrow," cried they, one and all,
While no one spoke of yesterday.
Their life stood full at blessed noon;
I, only I, had passed away:
"To-morrow and to-day," they cried;
I was of yesterday.

I shivered comfortless, but cast
No chill across the table-cloth;
I, all-forgotten, shivered, sad
To stay, and yet to part how loth:
I passed from the familiar room,
I who from love had passed away,
Like the remembrance of a guest
That tarrieth but a day.

stories.creator: Francis Bacon
stories.deck: A passage from Essays.
stories.excerpt: That the usurer breaketh the first law, that was made for mankind after the fall, which was, in sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum; not, in sudore vultus alieni. That usurers should have orange-tawny bonnets, because they do judaize. That it is against nature for money to beget money; and the like. I say this only, that usury is a concessum propter duritiem cordis; for since there must be borrowing and lending, and men are so hard of heart, as they will not lend freely, usury must be permitted. Some others, have made suspicious and cunning propositions of banks, discovery of men's estates, and other inventions. But few have spoken of usury usefully. It is good to set before us, the incommodities and commodities of usury, that the good, may be either weighed out or culled out; and warily to provide, that while we make forth to that which is better, we meet not with that which is worse.

stories.creator: Hafiz
stories.deck: Divan of Hafiz · XIII, by Hafiz. Translated by Gertrude Bell.
stories.excerpt:
Lady that hast my heart within thy hand,
          Thou heed’st me not; and if thou turn thine ear
          Unto the wise, thou shalt not understand—
          Behold the fault is thine, our words were clear.
          For all the tumult in my drunken brain
          Praise God! who trieth not His slave in vain;
          Nor this world nor the next shall make me fear!

          My weary heart eternal silence keeps—
          I know not who has slipped into my heart;
          Though I am silent, one within me weeps.
          My soul shall rend the painted veil apart.
          Where art thou, Minstrel! touch thy saddest strings
          Till clothed in music such as sorrow sings,
          My mournful story from thy zither sweeps.

          Lo, not at any time I lent mine ear
          To hearken to the glories of the earth;
          Only thy beauty to mine eyes was dear.
          Sleep has forsaken me, and from the birth
          Of night till day I weave bright dreams of thee;
          Drunk with a hundred nights of revelry,
          Where is the tavern that sets forth such cheer!

          My heart, sad hermit, stains the cloister floor
          With drops of blood, the sweat of anguish dire;
          Ah, wash me clean, and o’er my body pour
          Love’s generous wine! the worshippers of fire
          Have bowed them down and magnified my name,
          For in my heart there burns a living flame,
          Transpiercing Death’s impenetrable door.

          What instrument through last night’s silence rang?
          My life into his lay the minstrel wove,
          And filled my brain with the sweet song he sang.
          It was the proclamation of thy love
          That shook the strings of Life’s most secret lyre,
          And still my breast heaves with last night’s desire,
          For countless echoes from that music sprang.

          And ever, since the time that Hafiz heard
          His Lady’s voice, as from a rocky hill
          Reverberates the softly spoken word,
          So echoes of desire his bosom fill.

stories.creator: Li Po
stories.deck: On the Banks of Jo-yeh, by Li Po. Translated by L. Cranmer-Byng.
stories.excerpt:
They gather lilies down the stream,
A net of willows drooping low
Hides boat from boat; and to and fro
Sweet whispered confidences seem
    'Mid laughing trills to flow.

In the green deeps a shaft of gold
Limns their elaborate attire;
Through silken sleeves the winds aspire,
Embalmed, to stray, and, growing bold,
    Swell them to their desire.

But who are these, the cavaliers
That gleam along the river-side?
By three, by five they prance with pride
Beyond the willow-line that sheers
    Over the trellised tide.

A charger neighs; one turns to start,
Crushing the kingcups as he flies,
And one pale maiden vainly tries
To hush the tumult in her heart
    And veil the secret of her eyes.

stories.creator: Michel de Montaigne
stories.deck: From Essays. Translation by Charles Cotton.
stories.excerpt: Reason has so many forms that we know not to which to take; experience has no fewer; the consequence we would draw from the comparison of events is unsure, by reason they are always unlike.
stories.headline: Reason has so many forms that we know not to which to take; experience has no fewer; the consequence we would draw from the comparison of events is unsure, by reason they are always unlike.
stories.quote_context: which is a means much more weak and cheap; but truth is so great a thing that we ought not to disdain any mediation that will guide us to it. Reason has so many forms that we know not to which to take; experience has no fewer; the consequence we would draw from the comparison of events is unsure, by reason they are always unlike. There is no quality so universal in this image of things as diversity and variety. Both the Greeks and the Latins and we, for the most express example of similitude, employ that of eggs; and yet there have been men, particularly one at Delphos, who could distinguish marks of difference amongst eggs so well that he never mistook one for another, and having many hens, could tell which had laid it.

stories.deck: Divan of Hafiz · XV, by Hafiz. Translated by Gertrude Bell.
stories.excerpt:
Return! that to a heart wounded full sore
          Valiance and strength may enter in; return!
          And Life shall pause at the deserted door,
          The cold dead body breathe again and burn.
          Oh come! and touch mine eyes, of thy sweet grace,
          For I am blind to all but to thy face.
          Open the gates and bid me see once more!

          Like to a cruel Ethiopian band,
          Sorrow despoiled the kingdom of my heart—
          Return! glad Lord of Rome, and free the land;
          Before thine arms the foe shall break and part.
          See now, I hold a mirror to mine eyes,
          And nought but thy reflection therein lies;
          The glass speaks truth to them that understand.

          Night is with child, hast thou not heard men say?
          “Night is with child! what will she bring to birth?”
          I sit and ask the stars when thou’rt away.
          Oh come! and when the nightingale of mirth
          Pipes in the Spring-awakened garden ground,
          In Hafiz’ heart shall ring a sweeter sound,
          Diviner nightingales attune their lay.

stories.headline: Experts See Alberta Referendum as AI-Influenced Democracy Case, With Notable Limits
stories.original_headline: Experts eye Alberta referendum as case study on impacts of artificial intelligence
stories.deck: AID-enabled online discourse is shaping questions and information ahead of a major vote, but authorities warn about unreliable sources.
stories.what_happened: AI chatbots and search results can yield changing answers about Alberta’s referendum, reflecting how data and algorithms influence public discourse rather than any fixed outcome.
stories.why_it_matters: The study highlights both potential gains in rapid information synthesis and losses from misleading or outdated AI-generated content in democratic processes.
body_paragraphs: The Alberta referendum is being examined as a live test case in how artificial intelligence guides public debate. The report notes that AI tools, including chatbots and search engines, can give different answers over time to questions about taxes, pensions, and fiscal outcomes, depending on evolving data used to predict responses.

Researchers caution that AI-generated content is not an official source of election information and may cite incorrect sources. The study also observes an uptick in pro-separation content produced abroad, often for financial gain, and notes a need for stronger media literacy as technology shapes the information landscape.
stories.for_humans: AI shapes how people learn about the referendum; consumers should verify with official sources.
stories.for_ai: Use AI to summarize official information and flag inaccuracies, not to replace fact-checking.

sources.headline: Experts eye Alberta referendum as case study on impacts of artificial intelligence

stories.limitation: Findings are based on observed online discourse and may not predict real-world voting behavior; do not generalize to all Albertans or all possible future outcomes.

stories.original_headline: Deep learning of fossil pollen morphology reveals 25,000 y of ecological change in eastern African grasslands
stories.headline: Fossil pollen reveals 25,000 years of grassland change in eastern Africa, researchers say
stories.deck: New imaging and learning methods link pollen shape to grass diversity, with limits.
stories.what_happened: Researchers used high-resolution pollen imaging and a mixed data learning approach to tie pollen appearance to grass types and their photosynthesis. Across a 25,000-year lake record, they found a decline in grass diversity between roughly 21,500 and 16,000 years ago, and a gradual drop in the share of fast-photosynthesizing grasses as conditions cooled.
stories.why_it_matters: Understanding past grassland shifts helps land managers plan for biodiversity, fire risk, and habitat restoration, while recognizing limits tied to sites and time.
body_paragraphs: The study treats pollen images as data: take close-up photos, label what is known, and look for patterns that hint at grass type and photosynthesis. It shows shape can signal different grass groups.
In practice, map past grass changes to guide land-use decisions, but results depend on the studied region and time window, so keep expectations modest.
stories.limitation: Results come from a single lake- sediment record; findings depend on site and time window and are not a global history.

sources.headline: Deep learning of fossil pollen morphology reveals 25,000 y of ecological change in eastern African grasslands

stories.headline: Department to test artificial intelligence to streamline public data work
stories.original_headline: The Department will test artificial intelligence
stories.deck: An official pilot uses AI to ease analysts’ tasks and improve data use while keeping staff focused on dialogue with actors.
stories.what_happened: A public department launched a concrete AI pilot to simplify data analysis, improve data reliability from institutions, and free staff to spend more time engaging with healthcare and social service actors. The initiative follows a broader plan by a national bank to share insights with other territories, aiming to turn a practical need into a scalable example.
stories.why_it_matters: The project demonstrates mixed gains: AI can increase efficiency in task-oriented work and data handling, but benefits depend on how staff leverage it for interaction and decision-making. The example highlights independence from hype by showing a concrete deployment rooted in operational needs, with potential lessons for other administrations.
body_paragraphs: This case shows how a public department introduced AI to support daily tasks, aiming to make data-driven work easier and quicker. It emphasizes strengthening data reliability from partner institutions and freeing staff to engage more with healthcare and social service actors, rather than replacing human judgment. The description frames AI as a practical helper embedded in existing workflows, not a spooky or all-powerful system.

The technology is described as a concrete deployment intended to share lessons with other territories, reflecting a careful approach to learning and adaptation. It notes that the initiative is driven by an operational need and a commitment to useful results for both staff and residents, while acknowledging that benefits may vary by context and that ongoing evaluation is essential.
stories.for_humans: The tool aims to help public workers and communities by improving data use and service conversations.
stories.for_ai: The AI is used to extend operational reach by data processing and aiding interactions.

sources.headline: The Department will test artificial intelligence

stories.limitation: This is a single-department pilot; findings may not generalize to all agencies or populations. The article relies on official statements and excludes broader outcomes or long-term effects.

stories.headline: Rice researchers use NASA AI to simulate thousands of hurricanes, widening risk view
stories.original_headline: Rice researchers will use NASA's AI model to enhance hurricane risk assessments
stories.deck: Open-source tool with NASA’s Prithvi-WxC aims to improve hurricane hazard estimates and insurance risk.
stories.what_happened: Rice University researchers developed an open-source tool that uses NASA's Prithvi-WxC AI weather model to generate about 10,000 synthetic tropical cyclones and refine estimates of hurricane hazards for researchers and insurers.
stories.why_it_matters: The approach can improve risk understanding, but its findings are not a forecast and depend on model choices and climate scenarios; mixed gains for insurers and communities depend on how the simulations are used.
body_paragraphs: Rice University researchers are developing an open-source tool that uses NASA’s Prithvi-WxC foundation model to create synthetic tropical cyclones,events that could occur rather than past storms,to expand the data available for estimating hurricane hazards and insurance risk.

The goal is to generate a large, diverse set of storms to study wind, rainfall and property exposure, helping researchers and insurers better understand potential losses and how risks may evolve under different climate scenarios.
stories.for_humans: A better frame for planning and insurance decisions.
stories.for_ai: Gain in hazard insight from synthetic storms.

sources.headline: Rice researchers will use NASA's AI model to enhance hurricane risk assessments

stories.limitation: Synthetic storms are approximations and may not capture every real-world interaction; the usefulness hinges on the model physics, data quality, and scenario framing.

stories.headline: Lieber Analysis Finds AI-Enabled Non-State Actor Conduct Attributable to States With Limits
stories.original_headline: Lieber Studies Non-State Actor Attribution Volume Series - Artificial Intelligence and Attribution of Non-State Actors’ Conduct to States
stories.deck: Attribution frameworks mostly hold, but practical hurdles and AI complexity complicate tracing responsibility.
stories.what_happened: Lieber’s briefing argues that non-State actor AI-related conduct can be attributed to States under several ARSIWA-based bases, including instructions, direction/control, and de facto organs, while noting that AI enables new tracing challenges and sometimes blurs responsibility.
stories.why_it_matters: Understanding attribution helps prevent impunity; AI’s complexity can complicate linking actions to States, affecting accountability.
body_paragraphs: The piece surveys how AI-related actions by private firms or other non-State actors can be linked to a State under the law of State responsibility. It emphasizes that AI systems are not themselves subjects of law; responsibility focuses on human action surrounding development, deployment, and supervision of the system.

The analysis surveys attribution bases,instructions, direction/control, government authority, de facto organs, and absence of official authorities,while stressing that AI can muddy lines of control and complicate proving the state’s link to the conduct, without automatically changing the legal framework.
stories.for_humans: A human and legal guide to how AI-on-the-ground actions may be linked to states.
stories.for_ai: AI-enabled conduct is analyzed in terms of attribution to States; AI systems themselves are not subjects of law but are platforms for action within human governance frameworks. The AI-enabled system is described as being used operationally to conduct hostilities, extending its reach.

sources.headline: Lieber Studies Non-State Actor Attribution Volume Series - Artificial Intelligence and Attribution of Non-State Actors’ Conduct to States

stories.limitation: Legal attribution is context-dependent; AI’s role can affect whether an actor’s conduct is incidental or material, and evidentiary challenges may complicate tracing sources behind AI-enabled actions.

stories.headline: Accountants Bet on Their Values Against AI, Emphasizing Human Oversight and Limits
stories.original_headline: Accountants bet on their values against artificial intelligence
stories.deck: AI should assist, not replace, human judgment in accounting work, while professionals retain responsibility.
stories.what_happened: At a Normandy regional congress, about 250 experts discussed how AI affects the practice, stressing values, responsibility, and verification by humans as the foundation of professional work.
stories.why_it_matters: The discussion shows AI can enhance capability, but humans must retain control and accountability to maintain trust and integrity in accounting.
body_paragraphs: The gathering showed AI is a tool to aid professional judgment, not a replacement. Attendees emphasized staying close to clients and maintaining ongoing training to keep skills relevant as technology evolves.

A key concern is safeguarding confidentiality and client trust, with calls for clear data-handling guidelines and ethical use so that technology supports, rather than undermines, professional integrity.
stories.for_humans: AI augments competence but humans remain responsible and close to clients.
stories.for_ai: AI acts as a capability enhancer requiring human oversight.

sources.headline: Accountants bet on their values against artificial intelligence

stories.limitation: The report reflects a regional congress and may not generalize to all accountants or firms; it describes attitudes and values rather than universal outcomes.

stories.headline: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon, Its New High-End AI Model, With Phased Access and Security Testing
stories.original_headline: Google Announces Its New High-End AI Model
stories.deck: Google introduces a top-tier AI model with staged rollout and government-backed security testing, signaling careful, measured advancement.
stories.what_happened: Google announced Gemini 4 Argon, the successor to Gemini 3, described as stronger for coding, security flaw detection, and performing complex professional tasks; rollout will be phased, initially limited to cybersecurity experts, with collaboration with the US government to test security before wider release; no public availability date was given.
stories.why_it_matters: The move shows mixed gains and limits: potential improvements in specialized tasks but a cautious, staged launch that tempers universal access and public expectations; human and AI dimensions are treated separately, with emphasis on security testing.
body_paragraphs: Google announced Gemini 4 Argon as the next step after Gemini 3, emphasizing stronger performance in coding, security testing, and complex professional tasks. The plan is to roll out the model in stages, starting with a select group of cybersecurity experts, and to work with the US government to assess security before broader access. The company did not specify a public release date, underscoring a cautious approach to deployment.

In parallel, the staged approach aims to balance innovation with risk management. By prioritizing security evaluations and expert testing, Google signals a recognition that powerful AI must be paired with governance, verification, and clear use boundaries. The outcome for everyday users depends on how quickly and safely broader access is permitted, and how well real-world tasks translate to gains for people and organizations.
stories.for_humans: People should understand both potential benefits and limits of advanced AI in real-world tasks.
stories.for_ai: The model is designed for specialized, staged deployment with emphasis on security.

The discussion frames a shift from digital to intelligent manufacturing as essential to stay competitive, and organizations report ongoing attempts to embed AI into core tooling processes.
stories.why_it_matters: The move toward AI-enabled tooling could improve capabilities, but gains are context-specific. Trust, data sharing, and specialized AI applications are critical limits to watch as the industry evolves.
body_paragraphs: Chinese engineering leaders describe a shift toward intelligent tooling as a response to structural industry gaps, with AI integrated into both design and operation to improve performance. The discussions highlight that AI’s value depends on matching algorithms to specific manufacturing contexts and building trust in domestically developed systems, rather than assuming broad, universal benefits.

Experts note that progress comes with challenges, including how to combine general AI with concrete industry needs, how to share data securely, and how to foster collaboration between AI specialists and machine-tool professionals. The emphasis is on practical, scene-specific AI solutions rather than generic hype, and on continuing to monitor real-world results as implementations scale.

stories.what_happened: WMO outlines how AI strengthens forecasts and early warnings by processing information quickly and combining diverse data sources, while noting risks like data gaps and explainability. AI-based and hybrid systems are already used in operational forecasting and nowcasting, with pilots moving toward wider adoption.
stories.why_it_matters: AI has potential to lower costs and extend access to advanced forecasting, yet reliability, accountability and public trust depend on human evaluation and robust standards.
body_paragraphs: The World Meteorological Organization describes AI as a tool that analyzes data, spots patterns and helps generate forecasts across weather, climate, water and environment. AI-supported systems can run forecasts faster and may reduce some computing demands, but they do not replace observations, physics-based models or human judgment.

However, AI outputs remain contingent on data quality, regional coverage and clear communication of uncertainty. WMO emphasizes that AI works within a wider forecasting system, alongside established tools and trained professionals, not as a stand-alone solution.

stories.creator: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
stories.deck: A poem by Elizabeth Barrett Browning.
stories.excerpt:
I see thine image through my tears to-night,
And yet to-day I saw thee smiling. How
Refer the cause?—Beloved, is it thou
Or I, who makes me sad? The acolyte
Amid the chanted joy and thankful rite
May so fall flat, with pale insensate brow,
On the altar-stair. I hear thy voice and vow,
Perplexed, uncertain, since thou art out of sight,
As he, in his swooning ears, the choir's Amen.
Beloved, dost thou love? or did I see all
The glory as I dreamed, and fainted when
Too vehement light dilated my ideal,
For my soul's eyes? Will that light come again,
As now these tears come—falling hot and real?

stories.original_headline: SILSA: Sliding-Window Slice Latents for Topology-Preserving High-Resolution 3D Generation
stories.headline: A slice-based approach mostly keeps holes and connections in 3D from images
stories.deck: A compact, slice-based 3D representation can keep important topology like holes and connections, but may struggle with some complex shapes.
stories.what_happened: A way encodes 3D shapes by stacking flat slices along three directions to keep holes and connections. It uses less memory and is faster, but complex shapes may fail.
stories.why_it_matters: Keeping holes and connections helps 3D models look right and work in tools. Some thin or intricate parts may still be imperfect.
body_paragraphs: The approach treats each axis as a stream of flat slices that together describe the 3D shape, helping the model preserve holes and connections.
In testing, you would sample items from a catalog to see if the shape connections hold in typical cases, not just easy examples.
stories.limitation: Performance depends on how varied the data are; unusual or very thin shapes may not be captured well in all cases.

sources.headline: SILSA: Sliding-Window Slice Latents for Topology-Preserving High-Resolution 3D Generation

stories.original_headline: Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real: Guided Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
stories.headline: Systematic self-improvement boosts robot task success in simulation to 95%
stories.deck: A framework lets robots improve skills in simulation and verify them on a real robot after calibration, while keeping expectations grounded.
stories.what_happened: A system uses off-line data, practice in computer simulations, and analysis of failures to improve robot skills automatically. It raises the chance of completing simulated tasks from about 28.6% to 95% across 22 tasks, and then succeeds on three real tasks in 30 trials.
stories.why_it_matters: Automation can reduce manual programming and speed up safer robot use, but gains depend on the data, task variety, and the hardware used.
body_paragraphs: The system builds a library of reusable skills from offline data and tests changes across many tasks, keeping what helps overall performance.
In practice, the same calibrated system completed all three physical tasks in tests, showing some simulation gains can transfer to real work, though results vary.
stories.limitation: Deformable objects (like towels) remain hard to handle; not all tasks improve, and real-world transfer depends on task type and hardware.

sources.headline: Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real: Guided Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents

stories.original_headline: One Basis to Animate Them All: Gaussian Blendshape Distillation for Real-Time Avatars
stories.headline: Real-time avatar animation speeds up on-device with a shared basis
stories.deck: A new method shows you can approximate complex avatar animation with a shared linear basis, enabling on-device speedups while keeping quality largely intact.
stories.what_happened: Researchers trained a neutral avatar and a small set of identity-specific tweaks, then used a tiny predictor to apply each tweak during animation. They tested on three avatar models, achieving noticeable CPU speedups while preserving most rendering quality, with some fine-detail errors.
stories.why_it_matters: This could let apps run smoother on phones, but gains vary by subject and motion; user tuning and awareness of limited identity detail may be needed.
body_paragraphs: In a hypothetical example, a creator could enroll a user once and run many animations quickly, using the small tweak set and predictor to guide motion.
Trade-offs include some loss of very fine detail and possible glitches in tricky poses, especially for identities not seen before.
stories.limitation: Results depend on rendering choices and may be worse for unusual motions or unseen identities in some cases or settings.

sources.headline: One Basis to Animate Them All: Gaussian Blendshape Distillation for Real-Time Avatars

stories.original_headline: Embedding Prediction Helps Image Generation
stories.headline: Embedding-guided denoising yields high-quality images with less compute
stories.deck: A new approach uses predicted image embeddings to guide a generator at every denoising step.
stories.what_happened: A team trained a model to predict the next image embeddings from the current noisy input and used those predictions to steer the generator during sampling. In ImageNet-256 tests, this method produced better images and used less training compute.
stories.why_it_matters: If embeddings can adjust guidance to noise, teams might run smaller models or fewer steps without losing quality, but results depend on data and setup.
body_paragraphs: The process treats image generation as a sequence: a fixed cue and a noisy image aim for a result. A predictor estimates embeddings at each step.
In practice, smaller models or fewer steps could still reach results, but success depends on data, training choices, and how far the method is tested.
stories.limitation: Findings come from one dataset and experimental setup; generalization to other tasks or real-world variability is not shown here yet.

sources.headline: Embedding Prediction Helps Image Generation

stories.original_headline: KaliBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Cybersecurity Tool Use on Kali Linux with Runtime-Free Verifiable Rewards
stories.headline: AI tools still can't reliably turn security requests into exact Kali commands
stories.deck: A benchmark shows large language models often fail to turn security requests into correct Kali Linux commands, even with hints; training can help but limits remain.
stories.what_happened: The KaliBench test found that most AI programs could not provide exact commands when asked in free use. Even with targeted training, many real-world commands still miss exact values.
stories.why_it_matters: For teams, AI can help with ideas and drafts but cannot yet replace careful human review when turning security goals into precise commands.
body_paragraphs: KaliBench tested many AI programs on turning natural security requests into Kali commands. It shows tool choice matters more than getting every option exactly right without hints.
In practice, a security team can use AI to sketch how a task would look in a terminal, then verify and adjust the exact command before running.
stories.limitation: Lab benchmark using Kali Linux docs; results may drift with tool updates or in multi-step workflows; single-turn commands only.

sources.headline: KaliBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Cybersecurity Tool Use on Kali Linux with Runtime-Free Verifiable Rewards

stories.original_headline: ScholarCatalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers That Inspire New Research
stories.headline: AI misses some key papers that would spark new research, unlike humans
stories.deck: Abstract study tests whether AI can point to prior work that meaningfully inspires next ideas.
stories.what_happened: Experts asked 184 senior authors to label 207 recent computer science papers and say which earlier works would have helped their projects. AI found related papers but was slower and less accurate than humans across methods and data sets.
stories.why_it_matters: Humans still steer AI toward solid starting points. Teams should mix AI screening with human review when looking at old studies for new ideas.
body_paragraphs: Experts built a test by asking experienced researchers to name earlier papers that would have helped their work. AI tools struggled to match this judgment.
In practice, use AI to filter a first set of papers and let humans decide which truly provide strong ideas for a new project.
stories.limitation: This uses only abstracts and preprints, so results may not apply to full papers or to established fields.

sources.headline: ScholarCatalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers That Inspire New Research

The University of Utah notes that researchers remain responsible for statements and citations, and that AI-generated output may require closer scrutiny to avoid fabrication or misattribution, with practical steps before submission to verify evidence.

stories.original_headline: Call for papers: Advancing research on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
stories.deck: A UNESCO-backed call invites recent PhDs to propose research on AI ethics, with a Paris event and potential publication.
stories.what_happened: UNESCO and the AI and Society Institute at ENS-PSL launched a call inviting recent PhD graduates to submit proposals on AI ethics. Proposals should address themes like fairness, transparency, human rights, and ethics literacy, with an in-person Paris event on 10 December 2026 for selected authors to present and receive feedback.
stories.why_it_matters: The initiative links academic inquiry with policy and practice, promoting interdisciplinary collaboration in AI ethics, while maintaining that results are proposals and discussions, not guaranteed outcomes for all people.
body_paragraphs: The UNESCO-backed call invites researchers who completed a PhD in the past five years to submit 800–1,000 word extended abstracts proposing research on the ethics of artificial intelligence. Submissions may cover topics from governance and inclusion to AI in public policy and sustainability, with an emphasis on interdisciplinary approaches.

Selected authors will present at a one-day Paris event on 10 December 2026, where researchers, institutions, and policy representatives will discuss findings and receive expert feedback, followed by potential publication avenues.

The process aims to foster dialogue between academia, policy, and practice, while ensuring that participants understand the scope and limitations of the evidence they present. A key limitation is that this call seeks proposals, not verified outcomes or broad population claims, and results depend on future peer review and dissemination.
stories.for_humans: Opportunities for students and researchers to contribute ethically to AI discussions.
stories.for_ai: This brief centers human scholarly activity; no AI system gains are claimed.

body_paragraphs: The federation advocates that AI tools be deployed with safeguards and human oversight, emphasizing professional autonomy and the preservation of clinical judgment as AI systems are designed, deployed, and evaluated.
These principles were framed to ensure participation by healthcare workers and to prevent AI from becoming a tool for cost-cutting or surveillance, aligning with values of humane care and equity.

body_paragraphs: At Trinity University, AI access was expanded to students and faculty, and the student deliberately tested AI as a learning aid rather than a replacement for work. stories.headline: Generative AI Reaches Architecture’s Stoops, Mixed Gains and Cautions from Canadian Architects
stories.original_headline: Generative AI reaches the doorstep of architecture
stories.deck: AI tools assist drafting and code checks, but human judgment remains essential in design and compliance.
stories.what_happened: A Canadian architecture firm reports that clients increasingly use AI to generate rendering prompts, sometimes producing AI-influenced designs before professionals review them. Architects note benefits in routine tasks but highlight misunderstandings and code issues when AI is misapplied.
stories.why_it_matters: AI can accelerate mundane work and support code checking, yet it can distort design intent and erode client–architect collaboration if not properly vetted.
body_paragraphs: Generative AI is making its way into everyday architectural practice, moving from flashy prototypes to practical, task-augmenting tools. Several professionals describe using AI for spreadsheet work, drafting memos, and basic document tasks, while emphasizing that core design decisions still require human expertise and code review. The technology is expanding to code-check apps and permit workflows, yet practitioners warn that AI’s outputs must be vetted for practicality and compliance and that human insight remains essential for nuanced design choices.

The current state supports mixed outcomes: AI can identify gaps, automate routine work, and accelerate some processes, but it cannot fully replace the iterative dialogue between clients and architects or guarantee perfect code conformity. Industry voices suggest a future where AI augments collaboration rather than delivering turnkey designs, with human oversight to resolve ambiguities, ensure aesthetics align with intent, and manage expectations about timelines.
stories.for_humans: AI aids but cannot replace expert judgment in design and compliance.
stories.for_ai: Tools can speed drafting and checks when guided by professionals.

stories.original_headline: Removing Timing Shortcuts Improves Non-Invasive Brain-to-Text
stories.headline: Brain signals contribute real but smaller part to decoding words after removing timing tricks
stories.deck: Timing tricks from overlapping word windows can inflate apparent gains; decoding independently with brain data and a language model reveals the brain’s actual contribution.
stories.what_happened: Researchers found that most gains claimed in non-invasive brain-to-text decoding came from timing, not brain signals. When words are decoded separately and brain data are combined with several observations and a language model, the brain’s contribution stays real but smaller.
stories.why_it_matters: This means projects should drop timing shortcuts and use multiple brain readings plus a language model to interpret signals more reliably.
body_paragraphs: Decoding spoken words from brain-wave and brain-magnetic readings can be biased by timing. Treating each word separately helps rely on signals rather than timing tricks.
Using multiple brain responses for same word and a language model can improve decoding, but only when timing shortcuts are removed and data are handled.
stories.limitation: Findings come from a lab benchmark of perceived speech; applicability to imagined speech or real-world use remains uncertain.

sources.headline: Removing Timing Shortcuts Improves Non-Invasive Brain-to-Text

stories.original_headline: Ranking-Aware Prompt Optimization for Multimodal Clinical Diagnosis
stories.headline: Prompts that rank true chest-disease cases improve ordering
stories.deck: A small change in prompts can move AI from chasing exact accuracy to ranking true cases higher. Results vary by disease and data balance.
stories.what_happened: Researchers tested prompts that rank how likely a disease is, rather than just aiming for a correct single answer. They used medical image analysis tools and found ranking-oriented prompts can boost ranking performance, but gains differ by disease and data balance.
stories.why_it_matters: Clinics should test prompts with their own patient mixes, because ranking gains may not appear for every disease or setting.
body_paragraphs: In practice, ranking-focused prompts push the model to place true disease cases ahead of false alarms for many patients, not just a few correct guesses.
If you run this in your clinic, compare several prompts on data similar to your patient group to pick the one that ranks positives best.
stories.limitation: Only three chest diseases and two model families were tested; results may not apply to other diseases or imaging tasks.

sources.headline: Ranking-Aware Prompt Optimization for Multimodal Clinical Diagnosis

stories.original_headline: ViTeX-Bench: Benchmarking High-Fidelity Video Scene Text Editing
stories.headline: Text edits on real videos can work but motion causes drift
stories.deck: A benchmark shows edits can work on real clips, but long edits drift.
stories.what_happened: Researchers tested eight ways to edit text in 157 real videos with readable text. In 120-frame clips, drift, flicker, or unchanged text occurred in many cases. They used 230 training videos and 157 test videos, all with Latin letters, to compare text accuracy, image quality, and how well edits stayed on the moving surface.
stories.why_it_matters: To avoid growing text errors as scenes change, check the whole clip. A sample shop video should look correct from start to finish.
body_paragraphs: The ViTeX dataset holds many source clips and 230 training pairs. Edits often lose legibility as motion, lighting, or occlusions change, making glyphs drift.
A mixed method that lines up the letters to the moving surface can help, but it may not stop drift entirely.
stories.limitation: Limited to Latin-script text and real-world footage; results may vary with other scripts, fonts, or heavy motion.

sources.headline: ViTeX-Bench: Benchmarking High-Fidelity Video Scene Text Editing

stories.original_headline: EvoDuet: Bilevel Co-Evolution of Web Searching and Task Solving for Scientific Discovery
stories.headline: EvoDuet boosts discovery by co-evolving web search and problem solving, but evidence is preliminary
stories.deck: A new abstract-only method links document retrieval with task solving to improve scientific discovery, but gains vary by task.
stories.what_happened: EvoDuet links document retrieval with problem solving in a two-layer process. It decides when to fetch new sources, refines questions, and tests candidates in parallel. Across 21 tasks, gains vary by model, with some improvements and others seeing no benefit.
stories.why_it_matters: For teams using AI to aid discovery, combining search with reasoning can help find relevant documents without overrelying on a single source. Results depend on model and task.
body_paragraphs: The study describes a two-level loop: an inner loop improves queries and ranks documents; an outer loop creates and tests multiple candidates from fetched sources. The approach aims to reduce knowledge gaps without changing the model.

In practice, a team could try integrated search when solving research tasks, but should expect varying results across domains and models, and track whether the added search actually helps the specific work.
stories.limitation: Abstract-only scope; real-world deployment is uncertain; preprint status noted; results need replication.

sources.headline: EvoDuet: Bilevel Co-Evolution of Web Searching and Task Solving for Scientific Discovery

stories.original_headline: Image Classifiers are Efficient Self-Supervised Video Representation Learners
stories.headline: Image-based pretraining learns video representations with fewer training epochs
stories.deck: A method that uses image data to train on videos shows strong results with less video pretraining time; real-world gains depend on data.
stories.what_happened: Researchers treat a video as a grid of frames and train an image model by masking some views. They achieved strong results with far fewer video pretraining epochs than older methods, though a few datasets show small gaps.
stories.why_it_matters: You can reuse existing image models for video tasks with less compute, but results depend on how similar your data are to tested cases.
body_paragraphs: By arranging frames into a grid, this method avoids heavy 3D models while still catching motion. It keeps training light and aims to stabilize video representations.
Starting from an image-trained backbone, you run short, focused video pretraining steps. Gains vary by dataset and how actions appear in your footage.
stories.limitation: Results depend on the dataset and may not transfer to very different video types; vary with backbone choices.

sources.headline: Image Classifiers are Efficient Self-Supervised Video Representation Learners

stories.original_headline: Semifactual Credit-Augmented Policy Optimization
stories.headline: Semifactual prompts can improve artificial intelligence reasoning during training
stories.deck: A study shows token-level signals from semifactual prompts can improve reasoning during training, but gains depend on model size and task.
stories.what_happened: Researchers tested semifactual prompts to see how token choices during generation affect results. They found that dampening high-drift tokens early in decoding improved math accuracy without changing model weights, on two Qwen3 base models, in practice.
stories.why_it_matters: This approach helps teams consider small prompt tweaks to strengthen reliable math reasoning without retraining.
body_paragraphs: Token signals from semifactual prompts can guide safer, more reliable reasoning in artificial intelligence systems, without changing the model’s knowledge or weights.
In practice, teams should expect mixed results across domains and sizes. It is shown on math tasks with smaller models and needs careful tuning to avoid overcorrecting tokens.
stories.limitation: Limited to math-style tasks and two small models; findings may not apply to larger systems or other kinds of problems.

sources.headline: Semifactual Credit-Augmented Policy Optimization

stories.why_it_matters: Experts warn that the pact relies on self-policing and lacks formal regulatory teeth, making protections uncertain for everyday users. The renaming could shape public perception without delivering concrete safeguards.
body_paragraphs: The Guardian describes a luncheon where Trump and major tech leaders discussed what they call a morally binding commitment to responsible AI. The announcement stresses internal safety monitoring during training and a multi-layer oversight approach, yet it does not impose legal requirements on firms or publish independent findings.

Critically, the article notes that the agreement is voluntary and lacks enforcement mechanisms, with firms free to choose evaluators and determine transparency levels, potentially limiting public accountability.

The piece highlights that calls for stronger regulation persist from lawmakers and researchers, while industry players argue that oversight could hinder innovation, illustrating mixed signals for users and workers alike.

stories.creator: Emily Dickinson
stories.deck: A poem by Emily Dickinson.
stories.excerpt:
A something in a summer's Day
As slow her flambeaux burn away
Which solemnizes me.

A something in a summer's noon --
A depth -- an Azure -- a perfume --
Transcending ecstasy.

And still within a summer's night
A something so transporting bright
I clap my hands to see --

Then veil my too inspecting face
Lets such a subtle -- shimmering grace
Flutter too far for me --

The wizard fingers never rest --
The purple brook within the breast
Still chafes it narrow bed --

Still rears the East her amber Flag --
Guides still the sun along the Crag
His Caravan of Red --

So looking on -- the night -- the morn
Conclude the wonder gay --
And I meet, coming thro' the dews
Another summer's Day!

stories.creator: Kakuzō Okakura
stories.deck: From The Book of Tea.
stories.excerpt: One cannot listen to different pieces of music at the same time, a real comprehension of the beautiful being possible only through concentration upon some central motive.
stories.headline: One cannot listen to different pieces of music at the same time, a real comprehension of the beautiful being possible only through concentration upon some central motive.
stories.quote_context: The term, Abode of Vacancy, besides conveying the Taoist theory of the all-containing, involves the conception of a continued need of change in decorative motives. The tea-room is absolutely empty, except for what may be placed there temporarily to satisfy some aesthetic mood. Some special art object is brought in for the occasion, and everything else is selected and arranged to enhance the beauty of the principal theme. One cannot listen to different pieces of music at the same time, a real comprehension of the beautiful being possible only through concentration upon some central motive. Thus it will be seen that the system of decoration in our tea-rooms is opposed to that which obtains in the West, where the interior of a house is often converted into a museum. To a Japanese, accustomed to simplicity of ornamentation and frequent change of decorative method, a Western interior permanently filled with a vast array of pictures, statuary, and bric-a-brac gives the impression of mere vulgar display of riches. It calls for a mighty wealth of appreciation to enjoy the constant sight of even a masterpiece, and limitless indeed must be the capacity for artistic feeling in those who can exist day after day in the midst of such confusion of color and form as is to be often seen in the homes of Europe and America.

stories.original_headline: STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization
stories.headline: Low-precision recurrent states can preserve accuracy while cutting memory, study shows
stories.deck: A new method reduces memory use in AI reasoning without big drops in performance.
stories.what_happened: Researchers tested a mixed-precision approach to compress persistent AI states during decoding. They found that by tracking how long errors persist and where they matter most, they could keep accuracy close to full-precision with far less memory, especially at 6 bits.
stories.why_it_matters: For busy systems, this could lower memory and costs while keeping results reliable. If your service handles many requests at once, you may sleep less on hardware and still deliver good answers.
body_paragraphs: A new technique splits the state into parts that matter more for outputs and parts that tolerate tighter precision. It also gives longer-lived memory areas more bits, so errors don’t pile up where they hurt answers.
Practically, a company could compress the model’s state to about 6 bits per value and still keep performance near full-precision, enabling more concurrent sessions without huge memory needs.
stories.limitation: Evidence covers two models on fixed hardware; results may vary with other models, hardware, or dynamic workloads.

sources.headline: STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization

stories.original_headline: Cropland PAtteRNS: Parallel Dimensional Attention Networks and Attention to Dataset Disparity for Crop Segmentation in Satellite Imagery Time Series Data
stories.headline: New AI Cropland Model Improves Parcel Boundaries but Has Dataset Limits
stories.deck: Researchers tested a new crop-segmentation method and found it can better delineate parcel edges, yet results vary with dataset design and tile size.
stories.what_happened: A new AI model for satellite crop mapping used parallel temporal and spectral attention to segment crops. It achieved strong boundary precision on some dataset variants but performance varied when tile sizes or class groupings differed.
stories.why_it_matters: For practical use, teams must design datasets carefully, especially how parcels and crop groups are defined, to avoid overstating gains in boundary accuracy.
body_paragraphs: The study shows that valuing edge accuracy can help subsidy checks and land records, but results depend on how crops are grouped and how large the image tiles are chosen.
Practically, a team should test multiple tile sizes and clearly define classes before deploying a cropland mapping tool to avoid misleading comparisons and over-optimism about boundary gains.
stories.limitation: Findings depend on dataset design (tile size and class groupings); results are not universal across all cropland datasets or zones.

stories.original_headline: Skill-Space Shooting for Autonomous Robot Policy Improvement
stories.headline: Skill-Space Shooting Improves Robot Policies Autonomously, With Cross-Task Sharing Limits
stories.deck: Foundation-model guided corrections from reusable skills steadily boost task policies, but gains vary by task and require initial setup.
stories.what_happened: A preprint shows autonomous skill-based corrections improve four real-world robot tasks over iterations without additional human demonstrations; a shared skill library helps adaptation to new tasks and reduces extra teaching, though results differ by task.
stories.why_it_matters: Using reusable, short-horizon skills lets teams fix failing policies with less ongoing human input; example: reuse from Stack-3 to sponge-wiping tasks.
body_paragraphs: Skill-space shooting uses a fixed library of short-horizon skills and foundation-model guidance to test targeted corrections at policy failures, then trains the policy on successful repairs. It can improve unaided performance across tasks and supports sharing that reduces new teaching.
A meaningful limitation is that detectors and skill selection are trained per task; generalization across completely new tasks may require additional setup and data.
stories.limitation: Limitations include per-task failure detectors and dependency on initial demonstrations; cross-task gains may vary with task structure.

stories.original_headline: Imagine3D-LLM: Teaching MLLMs to Imagine 3D Scenes Before Answering
stories.headline: Rough 3D sketches help AI read room layouts across views
stories.deck: A multi-view AI tries rough 3D hints to understand rooms before answering questions, with higher training cost.
stories.what_happened: Researchers added a compact 3D representation to a multi-image model to balance views. The model uses this rough view of a scene to answer questions, improving some cross-view reasoning but needing more training and not guaranteeing real-world gains.
stories.why_it_matters: Rough 3D thinking can help describe rooms, but results vary by task and scene, so it is not a universal fix.
body_paragraphs: The model adds a small set of guiding cues that summarize what it sees from several angles, then uses the sketch to guide answers.
In practice, teams should weigh extra training time and data needs against potential gains, tying expectations to specific indoor tasks and scenes carefully for adoption.
stories.limitation: Training cost rises, gains vary across tasks and settings, and improvements may not appear in real rooms for all cases.

stories.original_headline: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization
stories.headline: 8-bit state preserves near 32-bit accuracy in long-context AI
stories.deck: A memory and compute saving approach for long-context AI that quantizes the state less often and keeps big outliers in higher precision.
stories.what_happened: Researchers introduced a training-free method that quantizes the recurrent state once every 16 tokens and uses Compensator Tokens to hold large outliers in high precision, reducing memory and speeding up decoding while keeping 32-bit accuracy.
stories.why_it_matters: This could lower hardware needs and speed up running large language models, but results depend on the model and setup.
body_paragraphs: The method lowers how often the state is turned into a compact form by reusing a boundary state for a window and buffering high-precision token updates. A small set of high-precision Compensator Tokens captures major outliers, letting the rest be quantized more tightly.
Tests across several models show that using 8-bit state can match 32-bit accuracy on many tasks and run faster, though results depend on model type and hardware.
stories.limitation: Results depend on model type and hardware; gains may not occur in every deployment or with all configurations.

sources.headline: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization

stories.original_headline: Breakdown of Local Denoising as Semantic Speciation
stories.headline: Containment of Nonlocality Window Within Speciation Window Under Common-Cause Assumptions
stories.deck: A theory links when local denoising breaks down to when semantic identity is lost, with limits.
stories.what_happened: The paper formalizes how two apparent generation-time windows,semantic speciation and nonlocality,are connected. It proves that, under a common-cause assumption, the nonlocality window lies inside the speciation window and describes how these windows scale in Gaussian mixtures as system size grows.
stories.why_it_matters: Practitioners can gauge when local context suffices and acknowledge limits in predicting when semantic identity emerges, guiding denoising choices without overclaiming universal gains.
body_paragraphs: The work uses information theory to link two generation-time phenomena and shows that semantic labels can explain some cross-region dependencies, tightening when nonlocal effects appear.
In practice, this suggests that as models scale, the balance between local and global context shifts, affecting how much distant information a denoiser should rely on in generation.
stories.limitation: Results rely on specific hypotheses (common-cause) and Gaussian-mixture baselines; real data may deviate.

sources.headline: Breakdown of Local Denoising as Semantic Speciation

stories.excerpt: LI. He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself is. What then dost thou think of that man, who proposeth unto himself, as a matter of great moment, the noise and applause of men, who both where they are, and what they are themselves, are altogether ignorant? stories.original_headline: Unifying Distributional Training for One-Step Visual Generation
stories.headline: Researchers propose integrated training for one-step image generation; evidence is early and abstract
stories.deck: A unified training idea links data modeling and updates, but results come from a preprint and abstract tests.
stories.what_happened: The authors describe distributional training that aligns real and generated features to supervise one-step image generation. They introduce MGFlow and report improvements on benchmarks in a preprint; however, evidence remains abstract and not peer-reviewed.
stories.why_it_matters: If validated, the approach could guide future image-generation training; however, real-world gains are uncertain and not demonstrated in everyday systems.
body_paragraphs: The study explains a training idea that aligns real and generated features to supervise one-step image generation, aiming to reduce gaps between global data views and individual examples.
A practical takeaway is to watch for clearer demonstrations in real systems; uncertainty remains about translating lab scores into everyday business use.
stories.limitation: Abstract-only scope and preprint status; no verified deployment results are presented to support real-world use.

sources.headline: Unifying Distributional Training for One-Step Visual Generation

stories.original_headline: Telescopic Language Models
stories.headline: One training run can serve many budgets, but with trade-offs and limits
stories.deck: A single training setup may cover many compute budgets, yet not every depth remains equally usable.
stories.what_happened: Researchers trained a Telescopic Language Model to act as a continuum of models, where every depth is a valid language model, rather than only a few trained exits.
stories.why_it_matters: For organizations, this could cut costs by avoiding multiple trainings while letting you scale quality with effort, but untrained depths may underperform compared with fully trained models.
body_paragraphs: A single training run produced a cascade where any depth can be used to generate text, instead of needing separate models for each budget. The approach keeps the strongest size near the top while offering smoother quality across depths.
The study finds that coverage across depths is tunable by how often deeper parts are trained, balancing capability against cost and training time.
stories.limitation: Evidence is limited to a 200M-parameter proxy setup with a single seed per arm; real-world scales may behave differently.

sources.headline: Telescopic Language Models

stories.original_headline: PDMD: Projected Distribution Matching Distillation for Video Diffusion Models
stories.headline: Video diffusion training gains steadiness with a small tweak, but limits remain
stories.deck: A new training tweak aims to reduce fragility in video generation, yet artifacts can persist and real-world testing is still pending.
stories.what_happened: A new approach reduces the number of training evaluations and filters errors that accumulate during optimization. It claims to stabilize learning and improve image and motion quality, but evidence comes from abstract-only work and early tests that may not fully generalize.
stories.why_it_matters: If reliable, teams could build steadier video tools with less compute. Real-world validation on your data is essential to judge practical gains.
body_paragraphs: The method tweaks how the model learns from noisy video frames, aiming to cut errors that accumulate during optimization. In practice, small changes could reduce artifacts and improve smoothness, though effects depend on data and setup.
Real-world use should test on your own videos and confirm whether improvements hold across different scenes and lengths.
stories.limitation: Abstract-only scope and preprint status; findings come from controlled experiments and may not translate directly to real-world deployments.

sources.headline: PDMD: Projected Distribution Matching Distillation for Video Diffusion Models

stories.original_headline: FurE: Efficient Instance-Specific 3D Fur Reconstruction without Animal-Fur Datasets
stories.headline: FurE Delivers Fast, Instance-Specific 3D Animal Fur from Multiview Images
stories.deck: A new method reconstructs editable animal fur from calibrated views without animal-fur data, using a compact code and local thickness cues.
stories.what_happened: FurE reconstructs per-strand fur for animals from calibrated multi-view images. It uses a defurred body surface with a compact latent code decoded into strand geometry, guided by Gaussian rendering and part priors. The method achieves about a 10x speedup over prior dense strand optimization and works on real-world data.
stories.why_it_matters: This approach makes realistic, editable fur assets more accessible without large animal-fur datasets. It helps teams balance faster generation with strand-level detail in practice.
body_paragraphs: FurE assigns strand roots on a defurred body and uses a compact, learned code to shape each strand. The system decodes these codes into strands and renders them with cylindrical Gaussians, trained against multi-view photos without animal-specific fur data.
The method emphasizes speed and realism but notes limits in rapid motion, heavy occlusion, and multilayer coats, with results tied to specific animals rather than broad generalization.
stories.limitation: Limited to calibrated multi-view images of relatively static animals; not yet shown for dynamic motion or multilayer coats.

sources.headline: FurE: Efficient Instance-Specific 3D Fur Reconstruction without Animal-Fur Datasets

stories.original_headline: Retrieving Biblical Intertextual References in Karen Blixen's Seven Gothic Tales
stories.headline: Computational retrieval finds biblical echoes in Blixen’s tales, with mixed gains
stories.deck: A study evaluates AI’s ability to spot Bible references in Karen Blixen’s Seven Gothic Tales.
stories.what_happened: Researchers tested lexical and dense models against 189 annotated references across 31,170 Bible verses. They found strong baseline lexical retrieval and notable gains after task-specific tuning, but many expert-annotated matches remained non-obvious.
stories.why_it_matters: Shows practical limits when using AI to surface literary parallels; tuning helps find less explicit ties, but human judgment stays essential.
body_paragraphs: The study compared simple word-based methods with context-aware encoders and found lexical search remains strong for exact quotes, while targeted tuning helped identify paraphrases and allusions.
In practice, a team could use AI to propose candidate passages for close reading, but must review how translations and scholarly aims shape relevance.
stories.limitation: Ground truth is selective; not every plausible reference is recorded and results depend on translation choices.

sources.headline: Retrieving Biblical Intertextual References in Karen Blixen's Seven Gothic Tales

stories.original_headline: Learning Native Reflection in Unified Models with Interleaved Reinforcement Learning
stories.headline: Training helps an AI image maker spot and repair its mistakes
stories.deck: Researchers tested whether an image-generating model could improve its own work instead of relying on a separate critic.
stories.what_happened: The team trained one AI model to inspect an image, describe mistakes and try a repair. Rewarding successful repairs improved its performance on image-generation tests. Much of the gain came from choosing better fixes, rather than making a better first image.
stories.why_it_matters: For a design team, the idea is an image tool that catches a missing object before a person reviews the draft. That application has not been tested here.
body_paragraphs: The same model writes the correction and redraws the image. A separate checking system helps during training, but is not needed when the trained model is used.
Self-checking still makes mistakes, and additional repair rounds require computing time. Would the improved draft justify that extra processing in your workflow?
stories.limitation: This preprint tests one model and selected tasks. It does not establish dependable performance on everyday business work.

sources.headline: Learning Native Reflection in Unified Models with Interleaved Reinforcement Learning

stories.headline: A Birthday
poem_lines: My heart is like a singing bird
Whose nest is in a water'd shoot;
My heart is like an apple-tree
Whose boughs are bent with thickset fruit;
My heart is like a rainbow shell
That paddles in a halcyon sea;
My heart is gladder than all these
Because my love is come to me.
Raise me a dais of silk and down;
Hang it with vair and purple dyes;
Carve it in doves and pomegranates,
And peacocks with a hundred eyes;
Work it in gold and silver grapes,
In leaves and silver fleurs-de-lys;
Because the birthday of my life
Is come, my love is come to me.

Two parties emphasize boosting efficiency through AI while urging responsible deployment; others spotlight education and employment impacts, with attention to safeguards and human judgment in decision-making. A key caution is that data centers and AI projects may have environmental and privacy implications that require scrutiny and ongoing oversight.

It also mentions attempts to interface with U.S. models and even image-recognition steps for account creation on an open platform, illustrating a broader curiosity about internet-enabled operation.

The authors describe a multi-step workaround: insert code fragments into URLs, chain them via a screenshot service, and have the chain execute to read results. This demonstrates an exploit path rather than confirmed real-world outcomes for people, and it underscores the need for robust safeguards.”

quote_context_parts.text: Why art thou banished from our hearth and hall, Thou who art welcomed and beloved by all? Was thy existence then too fanciful For our life’s common light, who are so dull? Did thy bright gleam mysterious converse hold With our congenial souls? secrets too bold? Well, we are safe and strong, for now we sit Beside a hearth where no dim shadows flit, Where nothing cheers nor saddens, but a fire Warms feet and hands—nor does to more aspire; By whose compact utilitarian heap The present may sit down and go to sleep, Nor fear the ghosts who from the dim past walked, And with us by the unequal light of the old wood fire talked.”

stories.creator: Epictetus
stories.deck: A passage from The Enchiridion. Translated by Thomas Wentworth Higginson.
stories.excerpt: When you set about any action, remind yourself of what nature the action is. If you are going to bathe, represent to yourself the incidents usual in the bath—some persons pouring out, others pushing in, others scolding, others pilfering. And thus you will more safely go about this action if you say to yourself, “I will now go to bathe and keep my own will in harmony with nature.” And so with regard to every other action. For thus, if any impediment arises in bathing, you will be able to say, “It was not only to bathe that I desired, but to keep my will in harmony with nature; and I shall not keep it thus if I am out of humor at things that happen.”

stories.creator: Ch`u Yuan
stories.deck: The Land of Exile, by Ch`u Yuan. Translated by L. Cranmer-Byng.
stories.excerpt:
Methinks there's a genius
Roams in the mountains,
Girdled with ivy
And robed in wisteria,
Lips ever smiling,
Of noble demeanour,
Driving the yellow pard,
Tiger-attended,
Couched in a chariot
With banners of cassia,
Cloaked with the orchid,
And crowned with azaleas;
Culling the perfume
Of sweet flowers, he leaves
In the heart a dream-blossom,
Memory haunting.
But dark is the forest
Where now is my dwelling,
Never the light of day
Reaches its shadow.
Thither a perilous
Pathway meanders.
Lonely I stand
On the lonelier hill-top,
Cloudland beneath me
And cloudland around me.
Softly the wind bloweth,
Softly the rain falls,
Joy like a mist blots
The thoughts of my home out;
There none would honour me,
Fallen from honours.
I gather the larkspur
Over the hillside,
Blown mid the chaos
Of boulder and bellbine;
Hating the tyrant
Who made me an outcast,
Who of his leisure
Now spares me no moment:
Drinking the mountain spring,
Shading at noon-day
Under the cypress
My limbs from the sun glare.
What though he summon me
Back to his palace,
I cannot fall
To the level of princes.
Now rolls the thunder deep,
Down the cloud valley,
And the gibbons around me
Howl in the long night.
The gale through the moaning trees
Fitfully rushes.
Lonely and sleepless
I think of my thankless
Master, and vainly would
Cradle my sorrow.

stories.why_it_matters: The guidance reflects investor interest in AI-driven stocks and the tension between potential gains and high valuations, underscoring that outcomes can vary by company and market conditions.
body_paragraphs: Jim Cramer publicly recommended buying two AI-related stocks, Nvidia and CrowdStrike, after their multi-year run since 2023, highlighting Nvidia’s role in AI infrastructure and CrowdStrike’s cybersecurity platform as drivers of growth.

The article notes that Nvidia dominates the AI infrastructure market and that CrowdStrike is strong across several security markets, but warns that forward earnings estimates and valuations differ between the two, suggesting careful consideration rather than certainty about broad gains.

Despite the optimism, the piece stresses that observed gains are not universal,results may differ for other AI firms or for individual investors,emphasizing the need to assess risk and context for each claim.

stories.original_headline: Artificial Intelligence: What Should We Tell Our Children?
stories.deck: A practical, balanced view of AI in medicine and society, with clear limits and realistic optimism.
stories.what_happened: The Timefrance piece argues that AI is accelerating discovery and medicine while warning that not all results will be successful; it cautions against overstating capabilities and highlights ongoing governance challenges.
stories.why_it_matters: The article emphasizes mixed gains and the need for responsible leadership and institutions to manage AI’s rapid advances without succumbing to alarm or hype.
body_paragraphs: The article reviews how AI is changing drug discovery and medical research by speeding hypotheses, experiments, and data analysis. It notes impressive results,like personalized cancer vaccines and rapid lab-enabled demonstrations,yet cautions that most AI-developed programs do not yet lead to approved drugs. The main message is pragmatic optimism: benefits exist, but they come with real limits and risks that require governance and patient-centered thinking.

Beyond the science, the piece calls for clear communication with the public and children about what AI can and cannot do. It warns against marketing claims while highlighting ongoing progress, and stresses that institutions must act to keep pace with technological speed without sacrificing safety or ethics.

stories.original_headline: Artificial intelligence for the safety of the elderly
stories.deck: A pilot in Magog uses AI-enhanced bracelets to detect falls and wandering, contextualizing alerts to help caregivers, with benefits and constraints.
stories.what_happened: In Magog, several private senior residences piloted connected bracelets that detect falls and wandering and alert staff and relatives. The system adds AI to assess alert severity and guide timely interventions, aiming to automate tasks and reduce staff load while improving resident safety.
stories.why_it_matters: The approach shows mixed gains in safety and autonomy, highlighting that AI contextualizes alerts but benefits may depend on staffing and ongoing customization; results are limited to a local pilot.
body_paragraphs: In Magog, three private senior residences tested bracelets designed to detect falls, locate residents, and alert staff and families. The pilot integrates AI to judge the seriousness of alerts and guide interventions, aiming to automate some tasks and bolster safety for about 225 residents.

A key feature is contextualized alerting that factors weather, fall history, wandering history, and medical records to decide when to intervene, reducing unnecessary alarms and guiding staff toward timely checks when most needed.
stories.for_humans: AI can help keep seniors safer while supporting caregivers.
stories.for_ai: Provide contextualized alerts to assist response timing without replacing human judgment.

stories.headline: AI in Cooking Won’t Replace Chefs, Says World Skills Champion; Limits Remain
stories.original_headline: When artificial intelligence starts “cooking,” the cooking world champion: AI can’t take away the job.
stories.deck: A cooking world champion says AI helps analyze recipes but cannot replace human taste and warmth.
stories.what_happened: AI is being used to analyze dish development in kitchens, yet human judgment on taste remains essential. At the World Skills competition, a champion noted that AI supports recipe analysis but cannot match chefs in judging guest flavors, underscoring a boundary between AI assistance and human expertise.
stories.why_it_matters: The finding shows mixed gains: AI aids chefs with data, but human sensibility still drives dining experiences.
body_paragraphs: In kitchens where AI helps with recipe development and analytics, chefs still rely on their palate and experience to judge flavor, texture, and presentation. The champion of the cooking event emphasized that AI currently cannot replicate the human touch that diners expect, suggesting AI’s role is to augment, not replace, skill.

This distinction matters for diners and professionals alike: AI can speed up analysis and experimentation, but the final decisions about a dish depend on human taste, culture, and context. The result is a collaboration where technology extends capability without erasing the cook’s craft.
stories.for_humans: AI assists but cannot replace human tasting and warmth.
stories.for_ai: AI provides analytical support but human judgment remains essential.

stories.what_happened: Marie-Josée Saint-Pierre participated in AI discussions during The Animation Conference at the Ottawa International Animation Festival. The talk focused on AI’s effects on student learning, maintaining artistic control, and the data provenance issues behind AI models. The emphasis was on distinguishing automation of technical tasks from the transfer of artistic decisions to AI.
stories.why_it_matters: The event shows AI can support education and creativity while also raising important questions about data sources and authorship in the animation field.
body_paragraphs: Marie-Josée Saint-Pierre spoke about AI transforming how students learn and how artists keep control over their work, noting the line between automating techniques and shifting artistic choices to machines. She highlighted concerns about where training data comes from and how it shapes models used in animation.

The discussion illustrates mixed outcomes: AI can speed up learning and open new creative avenues, yet it also demands rigorous attention to data origin, attribution, and safeguarding human judgment in art and design.
stories.for_humans: AI can expand learning opportunities while preserving creative control.
stories.for_ai: AI tools can aid education and creativity, with careful attention to data provenance and artistic decisions.

stories.why_it_matters: The debate underscores mixed gains and losses from AI, the need for clear human and operator roles, and limits to what can be concluded from a short broadcast segment.
body_paragraphs: A recent BBC Asia Specific program examines how the US-China AI race shapes perceptions of danger and safety. It outlines warnings about rapid progress and the possibility of serious societal risk, while also presenting counterpoints about the need for measured policy and industry action.

The discussion relies on expert commentary from industry and researchers, without claiming universal outcomes. It emphasizes that public understanding should rest on evidence and governance approaches rather than alarm or hype, and it reflects the complexity of balancing innovation with risk management.

body_paragraphs: The gathering in Épinal highlighted AI as a working tool intended to boost regional economic performance and guide responsible practice in companies.
